units.text: Mechanical Engineering Journal Key factors limiting carbon nanotube strength: Structural characterization and mechanical properties of multi-walled carbon nanotubes
Introduction
Experimental procedure

Spinnable MWCNT arrays were obtained by catalytic CVD method using C 2 H 2 and FeCl 2 as the base material and the catalyst, respectively. The procedure for the fabrication of the MWCNT arrays follows Inoue, et al. (2008). The length of the MWCNTs was ~700 μm. The MWCNT monolithic sheets were drawn out of the MWCNT arrays and wound onto a rotating plate (Inoue, et al., 2010), and then thermally-annealed in a graphite crucible (Kurata Giken SCC-U-80/150) using a resistance heated graphite element furnace at 2000˚C in vacuum followed by a heat treatment at 2900˚C under an argon atmosphere. The outer diameter, inner diameter and the number of tube walls of the MWCNTs are summarized in Table 1. TEM observation (JEOL JEM-2100F) showed that these MWCNTs possess almost the same geometric measurements such as the outer and inner diameters. (Observations were made on approximately 100 MWCNTs for each type.) The structural defect densities of the MWCNTs, namely the number of the defects per unit of MWCNT length were quantified by measuring the number of the structural defects in 3-5 TEM 2 For more than two decades, many researchers have focused on carbon nanotubes (CNTs) which have remarkable values for their Young's modulus, tensile strength (Peng, et al., 2008), electrical/thermal conductivity Lorents, 1995, Ebbesen, et al., 1996) and negative thermal expansion coefficient (Yoshida, 2000, Shirasu, et al., 2015, motivating their use in composites as a fibrous reinforcing agent. Recently, continuous multi-walled CNT (MWCNT) yarns and sheets, which are prepared by directly drawing MWCNTs from spinnable MWCNT arrays, have been developed (Zhang, et al., 2004(Zhang, et al., , 2005 and new processing methods utilizing MWCNT yarns and sheets have emerged as means of producing preforms and composites with higher MWCNT volume fractions (Di, et al., 2014). The Young's modulus and strength of CNTs are well known to depend critically on the structure (e.g. geometry, crystallinity and defect type and density) that depends on the manufacturing route and subsequent treatment (Salvatat, et al., 1999, Yamamoto, et al., 2010. In the previous studies, a wide range of modulus and strength values of short MWCNTs (~10-30 μm) have been measured, but no evaluation has been made for long MWCNTs (300 μm-1 mm) prepared from spinnable MWCNT arrays. Salvetat, et al. (1999) studied catalytic chemical vapor deposition (CVD)-grown MWCNTs that were found to have Young's moduli ranging from 12 to 50 GPa (mean 27 GPa), which is dramatically lower than the modulus of ~1 TPa measured for arc-discharge-grown MWCNTs. Yamamoto, et al. (2010) performed a study of the effect of acid treatment on the tensile strength of CVD-grown MWCNTs (~9 μm-long), using a piezo-actuated nano-manipulator. They found that the acid treatment decreased the strength from 20 to 6 GPa. Yamamoto, et al. (2014) investigated the tensile strength of 4 types of MWCNTs (~9 μm-long) synthesized by the catalytic CVD method followed by a series of high temperature annealing steps at 1200˚C, 1800˚C, 2200˚C and 2600˚C. The experimental results showed that the tensile strength increased for the MWCNTs annealed at higher temperature (7-21 GPa) over the ones annealed at 1200˚C (1 GPa). Yu , et al. (2000) measured the stress-strain response and strength-at-failure of individual arc-discharge-grown MWCNTs (~30 μm-long) under tensile loading. They reported measured tensile strengths of MWCNTs ranging from ~11 to ~63 GPa. In these studies, the tensile failure load was divided by either the fractured cross-sectional area (effective strength) or the cross-sectional area of the outermost layer of the MWCNT to calculate the tensile strengths of MWCNTs. However, only a few research groups have discussed the fracture strength in terms of the nominal (or ''engineering'') strength and the statistical strength distribution which are needed for the evaluation of mechanical properties of composites reinforced with MWCNTs (a detailed discussion is given in Appendix). Yu, et al. (2000) have calculated the nominal tensile strengths, and their values are in the range of 1.4-2.9 GPa. These values are in stark contrast to the effective tensile strengths (11-63 GPa). Thus, a fundamental understanding of the key limitations in improving the nominal tensile strength of the MWCNTs is essential.

Here, we present an experimental study in which we investigate the nominal tensile strength, Young's modulus and strength distribution of MWCNTs synthesized by the thermal CVD method followed by a series of high temperature annealing steps culminating with annealing at 2900˚C. These annealed MWCNTs possess a different nanostructure but with almost the same diameter and length. Structural-mechanical property relationships of such MWCNTs are investigated through tensile-loading experiments with individual MWCNTs, Weibull-Poisson statistics, transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations and Raman spectroscopic analysis. Furthermore, structural observations of the MWCNTs before and after their breaking are made using a TEM to identify the fracture location. In these TEM measurements, 20-30 MWCNTs were observed and the total length evaluated using an image analysis was 11-12 μm. Raman scattering spectroscopy (JASCO, NRS-5100) was used to evaluate the crystallinity of the MWCNTs. The measurements were carried out at room temperature under ambient conditions using an argon ion laser with an excitation wavelength of 532 nm. Five MWCNT monolithic sheets were used and the Raman intensity ratios (R) were calculated for each specimen, along with the average and standard deviation for each of the MWCNT type. Uniaxial tensile tests of individual MWCNTs were carried out with a manipulator inside the vacuum chamber of the scanning electron microscope (SEM; JEOL JSM6510) as shown in Fig. 1. Further details of the experimental procedure are described elsewhere (Yamamoto, et al., 2010). We measured the full cross-sectional area including an inner hole of each of the broken MWCNTs by TEM, and used the measured values to calculate the Young's modulus and tensile strength.

To identify the fracture location, uniaxial tensile tests on individual MWCNTs were carried out with a piezo manipulator (SANYU Electron) inside the vacuum chamber of TEM (JEOL, JEM-2500SE). A single MWCNT was clamped onto the AFM cantilever tip and a Si substrate by the EBID method of a carbonaceous material and a tiny speck of SEMGLU (Kleindiek Nanotechnik), respectively. The structure of the MWCNTs was observed in advance to determine the defect locations in the MWCNTs, and the tensile force was then applied to the nanotube. After the MWCNT broke, both cantilever and Si substrate with attached MWCNT fragments were observed in the TEM and the fracture location was identified.
Results and discussion 3.1 Structural characterization

First, we used Raman spectroscopic technique to investigate whether any structural evolution is occurring during the annealing process. In the Raman analysis, the graphite crystal structure has a characteristic peak at around 1590 cm -1 (G-band) while defective carbon materials have different peak at around 1360 cm -1 (D-band) (Dresselhaus, et al., 2005). Thus, the relative intensity ratio of the G-band to D-band peak, i.e., R = I G /I D , is known to depend on the number of defects in nanotubes (Kataura, et al., 2000). Raman intensity ratio (R) of the MWCNTs is shown in Table 1, where the MWCNTs annealed at 2900˚C (R = 23.3) appear to be higher R value than the as-grown MWCNTs (R = 3.2). This suggests that defects in the structure of the MWCNTs were removed by the annealing treatment to produce a more stable graphite planar structure.

This crystallinity change can be also observed by TEM. Fig. 2 shows TEM images of some of the MWCNTs prepared in this study. The as-grown MWCNTs consist of slightly undulated graphitic cylinders with respect to the nanotube axis (Fig. 2a), and they exhibit several types of structural defects such as discontinuous flaws, kinks and bends, and remnant catalysts (Fig. 2c-2f). The discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends were found in all as-grown MWCNTs, whereas the remnant catalysts were observed only in some of the MWCNTs. For the samples annealed at 2900˚C (Fig. 2b), the undulated structure disappears and the MWCNT consists of nested graphitic cylinders that are  Shirasu, Tamaki, Miyazaki, Yamamoto, Bekarevich, Hirahara, Shimamura, Inoue and Hashida, Mechanical Engineering Journal, Vol.4, No.5 (2017)   almost perfectly aligned with the nanotube axis, even though the structural defects such as discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends were still observed for a subset of the samples. The structural defect densities (the discontinuous flaws, kinks and bends, and remnant catalysts) are summarized in Table 2 for the MWCNTs prepared in this study. The thermally annealed MWCNTs show smaller structural defect densities of the discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends than the as-grown MWCNTs, and no remnant catalyst is observed.
Tensile properties and defects

The β values of the as-grown and thermally annealed MWCNTs are calculated to be 2.7 and 2.4, which is close to the data evaluated using the literature data for the previously reported MWCNTs. The comparatively low value of the shape parameter for MWCNTs indicates a wide variability in the tensile strength, more so than for carbon fibers (Okabe and Takeda, 2002) and SiC fibers (Curtin, et al., 1994) (β = 15 and 7-11, respectively). This may result from the irregular nanotube structure, which reflects a larger tube defect density relative to carbon fibers and SiC fibers. The present results and those reported for CVD-grown MWCNTs annealed at 1800˚C and 2200˚C by Yamamoto, et al. (2014) give higher nominal tensile strength compared with the other 5 kinds of MWCNTs. To help discover why these data show the higher strengths, Fig. 4 shows the dependence of the nominal tensile strength on the fracture cross section ratio and Raman intensity ratio. The fracture cross section ratio was calculated by dividing the fractured cross-sectional area by full cross-sectional area of the MWCNTs including the inner hole. The higher the fracture cross section ratio (for a given outer diameter), the larger the number of fractured walls in the MWCNT. The fracture cross section ratio and Raman intensity ratio of the thermally annealed MWCNTs was calculated from Yamamoto, et al. (2014). Fig. 4a shows that the as-grown MWCNTs used in this study and the MWCNTs annealed at 1800˚C and 2200˚C have the intermediate level of crystallinity as measured by the Raman intensity ratio (R = 1.4-4.9) compared to thermally annealed MWCNTs at 1200˚C (R = 1.0) and 2600˚C (R = 10.1). It is seen from Fig. 4b that the MWCNTs with the intermediate level of crystallinity produce complete fracture of nanotube walls and exhibit the higher nominal tensile strength. The slightly lower value of the fracture cross section ratio of the as-grown MWCNTs used in this study compared with the Yamamoto et al.'s MWCNTs annealed at 1800˚C and 2200˚C is owing to a larger inner diameter. Although the MWCNTs annealed at 1200˚C fail in the clean break manner (see Fig. 4b), their nominal tensile strength is observed to be very small (~1 GPa). The MWCNTs have a relatively lower crystallinity (R = 1.0), reflecting their amorphous graphite structure (abundant defects). When the annealing temperature is further increased up to 2600˚C, their crystallinity is drastically increased (R = 10.1) and an abrupt decrease in both the nominal tensile strength and the fracture cross section ratio is observed. This is probably because the number of load-bearing walls is decreased due to the limited load transfer from the outer walls to the inner ones, which may be caused by the removal of the crosslinking defects with the highly enhanced crystallinity, i.e. interwall sp 3 bonding (resulting in the multiwall-type sword-in-sheath failure and decreasing the fracture cross section ratio). These results suggest that a prerequisite for improvement in the strength of MWCNTs may be an appropriate interaction between the adjacent nanotube walls for sufficient load transfer to the MWCNT inner layers: not too low (but also not too high) to permit an adequate load transfer between the nanotube walls and thus a consequent clean break fracture. A detail discussion on the relationship among the nominal tensile strength, fracture cross section ratio and Raman intensity ratio of the thermally annealed MWCNTs tested in this study is described in Section 3.3. Of the 5 tested as-grown MWCNTs, 2 MWCNTs fractured at a kink and bend and the remaining 3 MWCNTs underwent failure at a discontinuous flaw. A series of TEM images for an individual as-grown MWCNT, captured before and after its breaking, are shown in Fig. 5. Note that the amorphous carbon accumulation shown in the images is produced during high-magnification TEM observation, but we have confirmed through the tensile loading experiment of the amorphous carbon that such amorphous carbon layers have no load bearing capacity during the failure of the MWCNT. By comparing the TEM images of the MWCNT taken before and after its fracture, it was found that the MWCNT fractured as a clean break. Additionally, the fracture of this MWCNT occurred at a kink and bend structure. Fig. 6a shows the key feature illustrated for a MWCNT fractured at a discontinuous flaw. This image reveals that the MWCNT failed leaving a very short sword and sheath failure as exemplified diagrammatically in Fig. 6b. It can be seen that the MWCNT has hole defects on the surface of its outer wall, and the fracture of this MWCNT occurred at a hole defect. These results suggest that the fracture properties of such MWCNTs are dominated by the above-mentioned structural defects.
Effect of annealing treatment

To further investigate the structure-property relationships of the MWCNTs, tensile-loading experiments of individual MWCNTs annealed at 2900˚C were carried out. The nominal tensile strength and Young's modulus of the as-grown and thermally annealed MWCNTs are shown in Fig. 7. The dependences of the nominal tensile strength on the fracture cross section ratio and Raman intensity ratio are also shown in Fig. 4. The nominal tensile strength for the thermally annealed MWCNTs shows nearly the same value as that of the as-grown MWCNTs even though a slight decrease in the strength is observed for the thermally annealed MWCNTs. Additionally, there is no apparent difference in Young's modulus between as-grown and thermally annealed MWCNTs. These results suggest that the structural changes observed over this annealing temperature range may lead to no significant impact on both strength and Young's modulus of the MWCNTs. As mentioned above, Yamamoto, et al. (2014) investigated the tensile strength and Young's modulus of MWCNTs annealed at 1200˚C, 1800˚C, 2200˚C and 2600˚C, and showed that thermal annealing is effective for improving their mechanical properties. The type of MWCNTs investigated by Yamamoto et al. had small defects, such as vacancies, Stone-Wales defects or crosslinking defects but no discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends as shown in the MWCNTs used in the present study. As a result, thermal annealing led to a decrease in the small defects with concomitant increases in both the nominal tensile strength (0.9 to 5.9 GPa) and the Young's modulus (38 to 480 GPa). On the other hand, although the as-grown MWCNTs used in the present study exhibit an intermediate level of crystallinity (R = 3.2), they include structural defects such as discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends. Such structural  Shirasu, Tamaki, Miyazaki, Yamamoto, Bekarevich, Hirahara, Shimamura, Inoue and Hashida, Mechanical Engineering Journal, Vol.4, No.5 (2017)   8 defects and the hole defects were not completely removed by thermal annealing (Table 2). Thus, the annealing treatments described here led to no major changes in the controlling defects and the thermally annealed MWCNTs failed leaving either clean break or sword and sheath failure (Fig. 4b). As a result, the thermal annealing had no significant impact on the nominal tensile strength and Young's modulus of the MWCNTs in spite of high crystallinity.

To make substantial advances in the performance properties of macroscopic CNT composites, the structure and properties of MWCNT yarns and sheets must be optimized at all of the hierarchical levels: from the individual MWCNTs, to bundles of MWCNTs, to networks of MWCNTs, and finally the macroscopic yarn and sheet structure. Future research efforts aimed at each of the following should be pursued to improve mechanical performance of CVD-grown MWCNTs (especially in the nominal strength): (1) developing synthesis methods for reducing structural defects (discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends); and (2) controlling the degree of inter-wall crosslinking and improving the load transfer between adjacent nanotube walls through modest thermal annealing. Conclusions

We reported an experimental study in which we investigated the nominal tensile strength and Weibull scale and shape parameters of the nominal tensile strength distribution of the MWCNTs prepared from spinnable MWCNT arrays. The main objective of this study is to identify both the fracture location during tensile loading of the MWCNTs and their strength-limiting flaw, and to evaluate the structure-property relationships of the MWCNTs. The nominal tensile strength and Weibull scale and shape parameter of the as-grown MWCNTs were 5.2 ± 2.1 GPa, 5.9 GPa and 2.7, respectively. The comparatively low value of the shape parameter for MWCNTs results from the irregular nanotube structure, which reflects a larger tube defect density relative to conventional fiber materials. Nonetheless, the values obtained in this study were found to be higher than those of CVD-grown and arc-discharge-grown MWCNTs evaluated in the previous study, suggesting that there was an optimal nanotube defect density for increasing nominal tensile strength; not too low but also not too high, so as to permit an adequate load transfer between the nanotube walls. It was experimentally shown that the nanotubes tested in this study fractured at structural defects such as discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends, which suggested that the fracture properties of such MWCNTs are dominated by the above-mentioned structural defects. We also investigated the effects of thermal annealing on the nominal tensile strength of the MWCNTs and demonstrated that the nominal tensile strength of the thermally annealed MWCNTs showed nearly the same values as that of the as-grown MWCNTs. This was because the remaining discontinuous flaws and kinks and bends may induce the nanotube fracture even though the overall structural defect density decreased with increasing annealing temperature. We believe that through the development of improvements in both synthesis and post-treatment methods, higher mechanical strength properties can be realized, and that through the production of a better defined architecture of CNTs, the electrical and thermal properties as well as mechanical properties of macroscopic yarns and composites would also be enhanced.
